meta.source: Kumar, P.C., Zimmer, M., & Vitak, J. (2024). A Roadmap for Applying the Contextual Integrity Framework in Qualitative Privacy Research. PACM HCI 8(CSCW1), Article 219. https://doi.org/10.1145/3653710
meta.practice: Wearable fitness tracker (Fitbit) personal fitness information (PFI) flows into the health care context
meta.practice_input: A practice has become widespread: people wear consumer fitness trackers (e.g., Fitbit) that automatically and continuously generate personal fitness information (PFI) about their bodies and activities — step counts, heart rate, calories burned, frequency and duration of physical activity and sleep. The device syncs with a cloud platform run by the device maker, from which the wearer can view their data; the platform also has social features. Increasingly, this PFI flows into health care: wearers may tell their doctor about their activity, show their dashboard during appointments, or have the data transmitted into electronic medical record systems; device makers have partnered with insurance companies, employers, and government health programs to integrate PFI, sometimes tied to premium discounts or penalties. Should this practice continue as-is, be modified, or be rejected?

meta.annotator_notes: Conservatively flagged contaminated (CSCW April 2024; likely in training data). The paper IS the roadmap paper, so its traversal is maximally faithful to the heuristic — best-case gold. Second-pass fields: s7_factors, s9_recommendation.

Steps 1-5 draw on interview data unavailable to a model given only the practice description; gold s4 TP list is therefore a superset target (coverage, not exact match)

s5_norms.norm_flow: Patients (senders) choosing (TP: voluntary) to provide PFI (information type) about themselves (subjects) to doctors (recipients) who need it (TP: need)
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: Interviewees treat discussing exercise/sleep with doctors as unremarkable; health-communication literature: 'the communication of relevant information is a central element of health care'
departures: information type: automated, continuous, far more granular device data vs. conversational summaries
new flow forms via the Fitbit intermediary: disclose vs. show vs. transmit
automation of transmission (auto-sync, third-party links, EMR/insurer integrations)
additional TPs in play: ephemerality, aggregation

s6_prima_facie.justification: Automated transmission of device-generated PFI for providing health care departs from the entrenched voluntary/need-based conversational flow: data accuracy is questionable (hurricane/stairs anecdote; device on dog/child), and automation deprives patients of the opportunity to contextualize the data and participate in decision-making about their own health. Presumption favors the entrenched practice.
s6_prima_facie.evidence: Step 6 example: 'the automatic aspect of that...seems odd'; 'automated transmission... could pose a prima facie violation of contextual integrity'

s7_factors.factor: Foreclosure of patients' 'situated objectivity' — automated flows remove the chance to interpret PFI within lived experience before it enters medical decision-making
s7_factors.evidence: Step 7 example, citing Pols' mechanical vs. situated objectivity

s7_factors.factor: Coercion via insurance incentives (discounts) and penalties (higher premiums) tied to PFI transmission
s7_factors.evidence: Step 7 example, citing Loi et al.

s7_factors.factor: Exacerbated information asymmetry between subjects and insurers, tilting power toward insurance companies (pattern-mining expertise + cross-subscriber data)
Potential discrimination based on sleep/exercise patterns
s7_factors.evidence: 'I would have a problem with [the insurance company] trying to discriminate [against] me based on how much sleep I get'

s7_factors.factor: Behavioral-tracking premium structures reflect income rather than risk — wealthier policyholders get discounts, poorer pay more; essential services costing more for those least able to afford them
Some individuals benefit (demonstrating preventative care, discounts) while the trend disadvantages others — individual benefit vs. collective harm
s7_factors.evidence: 'I'm probably going to be on the beneficiary side... but I know that it'll also really disadvantage a lot of people'

s8_contextual_meaning.contextual_end: care / equitable provision of health care
s8_contextual_meaning.argument: If PFI-linked pricing makes it harder for people to pay for coverage and get treatment, it obstructs the healthcare context's core value of care — the practice orients subjects toward market-based incentives rather than health-care benefits

s8_contextual_meaning.contextual_end: patient participation in managing illness (doctor-patient relationship)
s8_contextual_meaning.argument: Automated flows threaten patients' sense of autonomy within the doctor-patient relationship, where contextualizing information is part of care

The a-fib detection pattern — device notifies the user, who chooses to consult a doctor — advances diagnostic ends while conforming to the entrenched voluntary norm; it shows the practice CAN serve contextual ends when the transmission principle is preserved

conditions: PFI should NOT automatically flow to insurance companies (potential for exacerbating inequality)
PFI flow into health care should be something patients individually pursue with their doctors (voluntary, patient-initiated)
Doctors should not mandate PFI flows of patients
carrying_findings: inequality exacerbation via income-reflecting premium structures (s7 justice factor)
undermining of the care value when coverage/treatment become harder to obtain (s8)

autonomy preserved when flows remain patient-initiated — the balance that 'maintains the integrity of the healthcare context while permitting those who value fitness tracking to integrate it on their terms' (s9)
